lessons.title: Welcome to BE101!
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 1
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
BE101 covers how the web works, building pages, making them interactive, and connecting them to data. The tools: VS Code to edit, the browser to view, DevTools to inspect.

KEY IDEAS
1. Unit 1: how the web works (browser ↔ server).
2. Unit 2: building pages (structure and layout).
3. Unit 3: making pages interactive (clicks, input).
4. Unit 4: connecting to data from somewhere else.
5. Web skills can support a game: a landing page, a browser build, leaderboards and accounts.

STEPS: VS CODE HABITS
1. Open a folder, not a single file (File → Open Folder).
2. Use the Explorer on the left to see and create files.
3. Optional: File → Auto Save.

KEY POINTS
- VS Code edits, the browser shows, DevTools inspects.
- Web build vs. mobile build (for an app or game made in an engine):
  - Web: more technical quirks. The browser limits performance, file size and file access, and loading time matters. It's played from a URL, so it follows the same browser ↔ server rules as a website.
  - Mobile (Play Store): more setup and paperwork. Android SDK, signing keys, icons, a store listing and store policies. Once set up, the build itself is simple.

lessons.title: Clients and servers
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 2
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The internet is a huge network of computers. Clients (phones, laptops) send requests; servers (machines in data centers) process them and send responses. Every device on the internet is found by its IP address, like a street address. One page usually takes many requests.

KEY IDEAS
1. Client: the device you use; sends requests, receives responses, displays pages.
2. Server: a powerful computer in a data center; receives requests, does the work, sends responses.
3. IP address: the numeric address data is delivered to.
4. At home, your devices usually share one public IP through the router, and each has its own local address inside the network.

STEPS: LOADING A PAGE
1. The browser sends a request from its IP to the server's IP.
2. The server finds or builds the content.
3. The server sends the response (usually HTML).
4. The browser renders the page.
5. The page needs CSS, JavaScript and images, so more requests follow.

KEY POINTS
- Client → request → server → work → response → client shows page.
- In DevTools Network, each row is one request–response pair.
- 203.0.113.10 and 192.0.2.4 are reserved for examples, so no real device uses them.

lessons.title: DNS and finding servers
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 3
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
DNS (Domain Name System) turns a domain name into an IP address. It doesn't send the page; it only tells your computer where the server is. DNS happens first, then the page loads. Answers are cached for a while (TTL) so the lookup isn't repeated every time.

KEY IDEAS
1. Stub resolver: on your device; asks "what's the IP for example.com?"
2. Recursive resolver: run by your ISP or a public DNS (Google, Cloudflare); does the work of finding the answer.
3. Root server: knows where each top-level domain's servers are.
4. TLD server (.com, .org): knows which authoritative server handles the domain.
5. Authoritative server: holds the final records.
6. TTL (time to live): how many seconds an answer may be reused from cache.
7. A record = IPv4 address. AAAA record = IPv6 address.

STEPS: LOOK UP A DOMAIN (WINDOWS)
1. Open Command Prompt.
2. nslookup runescape.com
3. Read Name (the domain) and Address/Addresses (the IPs).

KEY POINTS
- DNS first → then the browser talks to the server.
- IP addresses change; a lookup today may show a different one than your notes.

lessons.title: URLs up close
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 4
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A URL has four main parts: the protocol (https://), the domain (www.google.com), the path (starts with /, like /search) and the query parameters (start with ?, key=value pairs joined by &).

CODE
```text
https://www.google.com/search?q=cats&lang=en

protocol → https://
domain   → www.google.com
path     → /search
query    → ?q=cats&lang=en   (q=cats, lang=en)
```

STEPS: BUILD A URL
1. protocol://domain
2. Add the path, starting with /.
3. Add ? and the first key=value.
4. Add more with &key=value.

KEY POINTS
- https://example.com/search?q=cats&page=2
- The path ends where the ? begins.

lessons.title: HTTP requests and responses
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 5
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Browsers and servers talk in HTTP. A request (browser → server) has a method, a URL and headers. A response (server → browser) has a status code, headers and a body (HTML, JSON and so on). GET means "just give me data"; POST means "I'm sending data to create or change something".

KEY IDEAS
1. Request = method + URL + headers.
2. Response = status code + headers + body.
3. GET: viewing pages, product pages, search results.
4. POST: signup forms, logging in, placing orders, contact messages.

KEY POINTS
- The method is always in the request; the status code and body are always in the response.
- Viewing → GET. Sending or changing → POST.

lessons.title: Seeing requests in the browser
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 6
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
DevTools → Network shows every request the page makes; each row is one request. Read the method, URL, status and details. Status codes are grouped by their first digit. Edits in DevTools only change your own view until you refresh.

STEPS
1. Open DevTools: F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I (Mac: Cmd+Option+I).
2. Click Network, then refresh the page.
3. Read each row's method, name/URL and status.
4. Click a row: Preview/Response = what came back; Payload = what was sent (for POST).

CODE
```text
POST https://example.com/api/chat/highlight
Payload: {"agent": "contextual-tutor", "conversationId": "..."}
```

KEY POINTS
- 2xx success (200, 201, 204). 3xx redirect (301). 4xx client error (404). 5xx server error (500).
- 1xx exists (informational) but rarely shows up here.
- DevTools edits never change the real files on the server.

lessons.title: HTML and JSON as response data
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 7
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS A response body can hold different kinds of data. HTML is page structure, and the browser draws it as a page. JSON is structured key–value data, and the browser treats it as text for code to use. CODE ```html
Box
``` ```json {"name": "Robert", "age": 25} ``` KEY POINTS - HTML → "I'll render this as a page." - JSON → "This is data; code can use it." - Some browsers (like Firefox) show JSON in a tidy viewer, but it's still data, not a page.

lessons.title: Setting up your developer tools
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 8
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
VS Code is where you edit files, File Explorer (or Finder) is where you find them, and the browser is where you view the result. Make a project folder with an index.html inside. The .html extension tells the browser to render it as a page.

STEPS
1. Create a folder called web-fundamentals.
2. VS Code: File → Open Folder → web-fundamentals.
3. Explorer → New File → index.html → save.
4. Check the name really ends in .html, not .txt.
5. Open it: double-click it in File Explorer, or drag it into the browser.

KEY POINTS
- index.html is the default main page name.
- A blank page is fine: the file is valid, just empty.
- Flow: edit in VS Code → save → open in the browser.

lessons.title: See HTML come alive in the browser
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 9
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Your first real page: a landing page for Elusion that explains what the game is, who it's for, its systems, the roadmap, and how to follow or support it. Next steps are tightening the text and adding links, images and styling as the course covers them.

KEY IDEAS
1. Strong already: what the game is (2D action RPG in Godot 4), who it's for, roles (tank, healer, mage, warrior), risk and reward, progression, economy and bosses, a roadmap, community and support sections.
2. To improve: cut repeated "hard but rewarding" lines; add the visual style and the player fantasy ("Become the..." / "Explore a world where...").
3. Later: links (Discord, YouTube, funding), screenshots or a gameplay GIF, styling.

KEY POINTS
- A page usually has one <h1> (the title); sections use <h2>. That helps screen readers and search engines understand the structure.

lessons.title: The life of a web request
lessons.topic: How the web works · Lesson 10
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The life of a web request: type a URL → DNS turns the domain into an IP → the browser connects (with HTTPS, a secure connection is set up first) and sends an HTTP request → the server returns a status code and body → the browser builds the page and loads the CSS, JavaScript and images.

STEPS
1. You type a URL and press Enter.
2. DNS: domain → IP. Failure: "Server not found" / DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN.
3. The browser connects to that IP and sends GET /products.
4. The server responds: 200 OK, 404 Not Found (reached, but no such page) or 500 (the server's code broke).
5. The browser parses the HTML into the DOM, requests the CSS, JS and images, applies the styles and draws the page.

KEY POINTS
- An error page or status code → a DNS or request problem.
- The page loads but looks wrong → a rendering or file-loading problem (missing CSS, broken HTML).
- example.com's IP address has changed over the years; look it up fresh.

lessons.title: Your first CSS stylesheet

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.topic: Building with HTML and CSS · Lesson 7
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Every element is a box with four layers, from inside to outside: content → padding → border → margin. Padding is space inside the border, where the background shows. Margin is transparent space outside that pushes other boxes away.

CODE
```css
.face {
  padding: 20px;              /* inside space */
  border: 2px solid #555;     /* width, style, color */
  margin: 30px;               /* outside space */
  background-color: #222;     /* fills content + padding */
  color: white;
}
```

KEY POINTS
- Padding grows the visible box; margin sets the distance between boxes.
- The background never fills the margin.
- By default (box-sizing: content-box) padding and border add to the width. Many sites set box-sizing: border-box, where the width includes them and padding squeezes the content instead.

lessons.title: Page layout with CSS
lessons.topic: Building with HTML and CSS · Lesson 9
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Block elements (div, p, h1, section) start on a new line and stretch across the page. Inline elements (span, a, img, strong) flow inside a line of text. display: flex goes on the parent, and its children line up in a row; justify-content spaces them along that row.

KEY IDEAS
1. flex-start: items hug the left.
2. center: items grouped in the middle.
3. space-between: first at the far left, last at the far right, equal gaps between, none at the edges.
4. space-around: equal space around each item, so the edge gaps are half the gaps between.
5. space-evenly: truly equal gaps at the edges and between.

CODE
```css
.main-nav {
  display: flex;                  /* on the parent */
  justify-content: space-around;
}
```

KEY POINTS
- Flex goes on the container, not the children.
- Used on the Elusion site for the nav bar and the rows of stat, follow and contribute cards.

lessons.title: The DOM: your page as a live tree
lessons.topic: Making pages interactive with JS · Lesson 2
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live tree of your page, built from your HTML when it loads. Each tag becomes a node with parents and children. DevTools → Elements shows the DOM, not your file.

KEY IDEAS
1. HTML file: on disk, edited in VS Code, changes when you save.
2. DOM: in the browser's memory while the page is open; can change without touching the file.
3. Analogy: the HTML is the recipe, the DOM is the dish on the table.

KEY POINTS
- A change that disappears on refresh was DOM-only.
- A change that survives refresh was saved in the HTML file.
- Clicking a node in Elements highlights it on the page.

NOTE

lessons.title: Selecting elements
lessons.topic: Making pages interactive with JS · Lesson 3
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Three ways to grab elements with JavaScript: getElementById("id") gets one element by id, querySelector("css selector") gets the first match, and querySelectorAll("css selector") gets every match as a NodeList. Each returns null (or an empty list) when nothing matches. console.log what you grabbed to check it.

CODE
```javascript
document.getElementById("game-frame");   // one element by id (or null)
document.querySelector(".enemy");        // the first .enemy (or null)
const players = document.querySelectorAll(".player");   // every .player
console.log(players.length, players[0]);
```

KEY POINTS
- ids are case-sensitive and must match exactly.
- querySelector uses CSS selector syntax: .class, #id, tag.
- A NodeList is used like an array: [0], [1], .length.

lessons.title: HTML forms and user input
lessons.topic: Making pages interactive with JS · Lesson 7
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A form wraps inputs and a submit button. <label for="name"> matches <input id="name">, so clicking the label focuses the box. name="..." is the key the browser uses: by default, submitting reloads the page with the values in the URL (?name=Alex&role=Writer). Saving or emailing the data needs more (a backend, a form service, or JavaScript + an API).

CODE
```html
<form>
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text">
  <label for="role">Role</label>
  <input id="role" name="role" type="text">
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
```

```text
http://127.0.0.1:5500/join.html?name=Alex&role=Writer&agree=on
protocol: http://   host and port: 127.0.0.1:5500   path: /join.html   query: ?name=Alex&role=Writer&agree=on
```

KEY POINTS
- for must match the input's id.
- Each query pair comes from a name attribute.
- A form with no method sends a GET to the same page.

The same HTML file can be private or public. Live Server (http://127.0.0.1:5500/...) runs on your own computer, so only you see it; use it while building. Netlify (https://something.netlify.app) runs on a remote server, so anyone with the link can see it; use it to share.

STEPS: NETLIFY DROP
1. Put an index.html inside a folder.
2. Open https://app.netlify.com/drop.
3. Drag the whole folder onto the drop area.
4. Wait for the URL (like https://peaceful-gnome-43f801.netlify.app).
5. Open it on another device to confirm it's live.

KEY POINTS
- 127.0.0.1 / localhost = your own machine, private.
- .netlify.app = public hosting.

lessons.topic: Connecting to data · Lesson 8
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
How the country app works, in one line: user action → fetch sends an HTTP request → the server responds with JSON → JavaScript reads it → the DOM updates the card.

STEPS
1. The user types a country and clicks the button; the event handler runs.
2. fetch(url) sends the HTTP request ("give me data about this country").
3. await fetch waits for the response: status, headers and a JSON body.
4. await response.json() turns the body into JavaScript data.
5. The code reads data[0].name.common, data[0].capital[0] and data[0].region.
6. It sets those on the card's elements with textContent.

KEY POINTS
- Request: browser → server. Response: server → browser.
- The page never reloads; only the card's text changes.

CORRECTION
The notes' DOM example used data.name, data.capital and data.region. The API returns an array with nested fields, so the working names are data[0].name.common, data[0].capital[0] and data[0].region.
